content: Water is essential for plants. Roots absorb water from the soil through tiny root hairs. The water travels up the stem through tubes called xylem to all parts of the plant. Plants use water for photosynthesis, to transport nutrients, and to keep their cells firm and upright. If a plant does not get enough water, it wilts because the cells lose their firmness. Plants lose water through their leaves in a process called transpiration.

title: Fruits: Nature's Sweet Packages
content: Fruits are the parts of plants that contain seeds. They develop from flowers after pollination. Fruits protect the seeds and help spread them. Some fruits are sweet and attract animals to eat them. The seeds pass through the animal's digestive system and are deposited elsewhere. Other fruits are designed to burst open and scatter seeds, like pea pods. Berries, apples, and oranges are all fruits.

title: Why Leaves Change Color
content: In autumn, many trees put on a spectacular show of color. Leaves contain green chlorophyll for photosynthesis, but they also have other pigments like carotenoids and anthocyanins. In spring and summer, the green chlorophyll hides these other colors. As days get shorter and colder in autumn, trees stop making chlorophyll and it breaks down. The hidden colors are revealed, creating beautiful red, orange, and yellow leaves.

title: Mushrooms: Fungi That Look Like Plants
content: Mushrooms are not plants - they are fungi. Unlike plants, fungi cannot make their own food through photosynthesis because they do not have chlorophyll. Instead, mushrooms break down dead organic material and absorb nutrients. The mushroom we see above ground is just the fruiting body. The main part of the fungus is a network of tiny threads called mycelium growing underground or inside dead wood.

title: Cacti: Desert Survivors
content: Cacti are plants that have adapted to survive in dry deserts. Their thick stems store water like a tank. Instead of leaves, cacti have sharp spines that protect them from animals and reduce water loss. Their roots spread wide and shallow to catch any rainfall quickly. Some cacti can go for years without water. The saguaro cactus can grow over 12 meters tall and live for 200 years.

title: How Plants Help Us
content: Plants are essential for human life in countless ways. They produce the oxygen we breathe through photosynthesis. They provide food - fruits, vegetables, grains, and nuts. Wood from trees gives us houses, furniture, and paper. Many medicines come from plants, like aspirin from willow bark. Cotton plants give us clothing fibers. Plants also help clean the air, prevent soil erosion, and keep our environment cool.

title: Pollination: How Plants Reproduce
content: Pollination is how flowering plants reproduce. Pollen from the male part of a flower must reach the female part of another flower of the same species. Some plants use wind to carry their pollen, like grasses and oak trees. Others rely on animals. Bees are the most important pollinators - they visit flowers for nectar and pollen sticks to their bodies. Butterflies, moths, birds, and bats also pollinate.

title: Seed Dispersal: Traveling Seeds
content: Plants need their seeds to travel away from the parent plant to find space and resources. Seeds are dispersed in many clever ways. Some seeds float on wind, like dandelion parachutes and maple samaras. Others float on water, like coconuts. Some seeds hitchhike on animal fur with hooks or burrs. Animals eat fruits and the seeds pass through their digestive systems. Some seed pods explode, flinging seeds away.

title: Carnivorous Plants: Plants That Eat Insects
content: Carnivorous plants have adapted to grow in nutrient-poor soil by catching and digesting insects. The Venus flytrap has leaves that snap shut when trigger hairs are touched. Pitcher plants have deep, slippery tubes filled with digestive fluid. Sundews have sticky tentacles that trap insects like glue. These plants still photosynthesize but get extra nutrients like nitrogen from their prey.

title: Edible Plant Parts We Eat
content: We eat different parts of plants. Roots we eat include carrots, potatoes, and radishes. Stems we eat include celery, asparagus, and rhubarb. Leaves we eat include lettuce, spinach, and cabbage. Flowers we eat include broccoli, cauliflower, and artichokes. Fruits we eat include apples, tomatoes, and strawberries. Seeds we eat include beans, peas, corn, and rice. Eating a variety of plant parts gives us important vitamins and minerals.

title: How Plants Defend Themselves
content: Plants cannot run away from danger, so they have developed clever defenses. Thorns and spines, like those on roses and cacti, discourage animals from eating them. Some plants produce poisonous chemicals - poison ivy causes a painful rash, and the castor bean plant produces deadly ricin. Other plants use bad tastes or smells. Some mimic the appearance of other plants to avoid being eaten.

title: Medicinal Plants
content: Many important medicines come from plants. Willow bark contains salicin, which was used to develop aspirin. The foxglove plant provides digitalis, which helps treat heart conditions. The cinchona tree gives us quinine to treat malaria. The Pacific yew tree produces taxol, a cancer-fighting drug. Traditional medicine systems around the world use thousands of plant species. Scientists continue to search rainforests for new medicinal plants.

title: Plants and Seasons
content: Plants respond to changing seasons in remarkable ways. In spring, warmer temperatures and longer days trigger plants to grow and flower. Many trees produce new leaves. Summer is a time of rapid growth and fruiting. In autumn, days grow shorter and some trees lose their leaves to conserve water. Many plants die back to the ground. In winter, perennial plants become dormant, surviving underground until spring returns.

title: Plants We Eat as Grains
content: Grains are the seeds of grass plants and are a major source of food for people around the world. Wheat is used to make bread, pasta, and cakes. Rice is a staple food for more than half the world's population. Corn, also called maize, is used in many foods and also for animal feed. Oats, barley, and rye are other important grains. Grains provide carbohydrates for energy, as well as fiber, vitamins, and minerals.

title: The Importance of Bees for Plants
content: Bees and plants have a special relationship called mutualism. Bees visit flowers to collect nectar, which they turn into honey. While visiting flowers, pollen from the male parts of the flower sticks to the bee's body. When the bee moves to the next flower, some pollen rubs off onto the female parts, pollinating the flower. This allows the plant to produce seeds and fruit. About one-third of the food we eat depends on bee pollination.

title: The Skeleton: Your Body's Framework
content: The human skeleton is made of 206 bones that support your body and protect your organs. The skull protects your brain, the rib cage protects your heart and lungs, and the spine protects your spinal cord. Bones are living tissue that grow and repair themselves. They store minerals like calcium. Joints are where two bones meet, allowing movement. Cartilage cushions the ends of bones so they do not rub together.

title: The Heart: Your Body's Pump
content: Your heart is a powerful muscle about the size of your fist. It beats about 100,000 times each day, pumping blood through your body. The heart has four chambers: two atria on top and two ventricles on bottom. It pumps oxygen-rich blood to your body through arteries and receives oxygen-poor blood back through veins. Your heart rate changes depending on your activity level. Exercise makes your heart stronger.

title: The Brain: Your Body's Computer
content: Your brain is the control center of your body. It weighs about 1.4 kilograms and contains around 100 billion neurons. The brain has three main parts: the cerebrum controls thinking, memory, and voluntary movement; the cerebellum controls balance and coordination; and the brainstem controls automatic functions like breathing and heartbeat. Different areas of the brain handle different tasks. The brain uses about 20 percent of your body's energy.

title: The Lungs: Breathing Life
content: Your lungs are two spongy organs that allow you to breathe. When you inhale, your diaphragm moves down and air fills your lungs. Oxygen passes from the lungs into your bloodstream. When you exhale, your diaphragm moves up and carbon dioxide leaves your body. Your lungs contain about 600 million tiny air sacs called alveoli, which provide a huge surface area for gas exchange. You take about 20,000 breaths each day.

title: The Digestive System
content: Digestion is how your body breaks down food into nutrients. It starts in your mouth, where teeth grind food and saliva begins breaking it down. The food travels down the esophagus to the stomach, where stomach acids and enzymes further digest it. Then it moves to the small intestine, where nutrients are absorbed into the blood. The large intestine absorbs water, and waste is eliminated. The whole process takes about 24 to 72 hours.

title: The Five Senses
content: Humans have five main senses that help us understand the world. Sight uses our eyes to detect light and color. Hearing uses our ears to detect sound waves. Touch uses our skin to feel pressure, temperature, and pain. Taste uses our tongue to detect sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami flavors. Smell uses our nose to detect chemicals in the air. These senses send signals to our brain for interpretation.

title: Skin: Your Body's Largest Organ
content: Your skin is the largest organ in your body, covering about 2 square meters. It has three layers: the epidermis on top, the dermis in the middle, and the hypodermis at the bottom. Skin protects your body from germs, UV rays, and injury. It helps regulate body temperature by sweating and shivering. Your skin contains millions of nerve endings that allow you to feel touch, pressure, heat, cold, and pain. You shed about 40,000 skin cells every minute.

title: Teeth: More Than Just a Smile
content: Humans have two sets of teeth in their lifetime. Baby teeth, also called primary teeth, start coming in around 6 months old. There are 20 baby teeth. They fall out starting around age 6 and are replaced by 32 permanent teeth. Different types of teeth have different jobs: incisors cut food, canines tear food, and molars grind food. Teeth are made of enamel, the hardest substance in the human body. Brushing and flossing keep teeth healthy.

title: Blood: Your Body's Transport System
content: Blood is a specialized fluid that carries oxygen, nutrients, and waste throughout your body. An adult has about 5 liters of blood. Blood is made of red blood cells that carry oxygen, white blood cells that fight infection, platelets that help clotting, and plasma, the liquid part. Red blood cells live about 120 days. Your bone marrow produces millions of new blood cells every second. Blood type is determined by markers on red blood cells.

title: Muscles: How We Move
content: Your body has over 600 muscles that help you move, breathe, and pump blood. Skeletal muscles are attached to bones and are under your conscious control. Smooth muscles work automatically in your digestive system and blood vessels. Cardiac muscle is found only in your heart. Muscles work in pairs - when one contracts, the other relaxes. Your biggest muscle is the gluteus maximus, and your smallest is the stapedius in your ear.

title: The Immune System: Your Body's Defender
content: Your immune system protects you from germs like bacteria and viruses. White blood cells are the main soldiers of your immune system. When a germ enters your body, white blood cells identify and destroy it. Your body remembers past infections through memory cells, which is why you usually only get diseases like chickenpox once. Vaccines help your immune system learn to fight diseases without getting sick. Fever is a sign your immune system is working.

title: Why We Need to Eat Healthy Food
content: Food gives your body energy and nutrients to grow and function. Carbohydrates like bread and rice give you energy. Proteins like meat, eggs, and beans help build and repair muscles. Fats provide energy and help absorb vitamins. Vitamins and minerals keep your body working properly - vitamin C helps healing, calcium strengthens bones, and iron helps your blood carry oxygen. Eating a balanced diet with fruits, vegetables, proteins, and grains is important.

title: The Nervous System
content: Your nervous system is a network of nerves that carries messages between your brain and the rest of your body. It has two main parts: the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (nerves throughout your body). Neurons are the cells that transmit these messages as electrical signals. Some nerve signals travel at speeds up to 120 meters per second. Reflexes are automatic responses that happen without thinking.

title: How Your Bones Grow
content: When you were born, your body had about 300 bones. As you grow, some of these bones fuse together, so an adult has 206 bones. Bones grow longer at special areas called growth plates, which are found near the ends of long bones. The growth plates are made of cartilage that gradually turns into bone. This process continues until you stop growing, usually in your late teens or early twenties. Calcium and vitamin D are important for bone growth.

title: The Eye: How We See
content: Your eyes are amazing organs that detect light and convert it into signals your brain can understand. Light enters through the cornea, passes through the pupil, and is focused by the lens onto the retina at the back of the eye. The retina contains millions of light-sensitive cells called rods and cones. Rods help you see in dim light, and cones detect color. The optic nerve carries visual information to your brain, which interprets what you see.

title: The Ear: How We Hear
content: Your ears do two important jobs: hearing and balance. Sound waves enter the outer ear and travel down the ear canal to the eardrum, which vibrates. Three tiny bones in the middle ear - the hammer, anvil, and stirrup - amplify these vibrations. In the inner ear, the cochlea converts vibrations into electrical signals sent to the brain. The semicircular canals in your inner ear help you keep your balance. Loud noises can damage your hearing permanently.

title: Why Do We Sleep?
content: Sleep is essential for your health and well-being. During sleep, your brain processes information from the day and forms memories. Your body repairs tissues and releases growth hormones. Most children need 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night. Sleep has different stages, including REM sleep when you dream. Without enough sleep, you may have trouble concentrating, feel irritable, and get sick more often. Good sleep habits include a regular bedtime routine.

title: The Kidneys: Your Body's Filters
content: Your kidneys are two bean-shaped organs about the size of your fist, located near the middle of your back. They filter waste products and excess water from your blood to produce urine. Every day, your kidneys filter about 180 liters of blood. They also help regulate blood pressure, produce red blood cells, and maintain the balance of minerals like sodium and potassium. Drinking enough water helps your kidneys work properly.

title: Exercise and Your Body
content: Regular exercise is important for a healthy body. It strengthens your heart and lungs, builds strong muscles and bones, and helps maintain a healthy weight. Exercise also improves your mood by releasing chemicals called endorphins. Different types of exercise have different benefits: aerobic exercise like running improves your heart and lungs; strength exercises like push-ups build muscles; and stretching improves flexibility. Children should get at least 60 minutes of physical activity each day.

title: The Liver: Your Body's Chemical Factory
content: Your liver is the largest internal organ, weighing about 1.4 kilograms. It performs over 500 different functions. The liver filters toxins from your blood, produces bile to help digest fats, stores vitamins and minerals, and helps regulate blood sugar levels. It processes medications and breaks down old red blood cells. The liver can regenerate itself - if part of it is removed, it can grow back to its original size. Your liver works constantly to keep your body healthy.

title: Water and Your Body
content: About 60 percent of your body is water. Water is essential for almost every body function. It helps digest food, transport nutrients, regulate body temperature, and remove waste. Your brain and heart are about 73 percent water. You lose water throughout the day through breathing, sweating, and going to the bathroom. You need to drink water to replace what you lose. Feeling thirsty is a sign that your body needs water. Drinking enough water helps you think and play better.

title: The Respiratory System
content: Your respiratory system brings oxygen into your body and removes carbon dioxide. Air enters through your nose or mouth, travels down the trachea, and then goes into bronchi that lead to your lungs. The lungs contain tiny air sacs called alveoli where oxygen passes into your blood. The diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle below your lungs, helps you breathe in and out. Your respiratory rate changes with activity - it increases when you exercise to bring in more oxygen.

title: Handwashing and Germs
content: Washing your hands is one of the best ways to prevent getting sick. Germs like bacteria and viruses can live on surfaces and transfer to your hands when you touch them. When you touch your face, eyes, or mouth, these germs can enter your body. You should wash your hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, especially after using the bathroom, before eating, and after coughing or sneezing. Handwashing prevents the spread of illnesses like colds and flu.

title: Allergies: When Your Body Overreacts
content: An allergy is when your immune system reacts to a harmless substance as if it were dangerous. Common allergens include pollen, dust mites, pet dander, certain foods like peanuts, and insect stings. When an allergic person encounters an allergen, their body releases histamine, causing symptoms like sneezing, itching, watery eyes, or rashes. Some allergies can be severe, causing a reaction called anaphylaxis. Antihistamines and allergy shots can help manage allergies.

title: Growing and Changing
content: Your body changes as you grow. Babies grow quickly, doubling their birth weight by about 5 months. Children grow steadily, gaining about 5 to 6 centimeters each year. During puberty, usually between ages 8 and 14, your body goes through many changes as it matures into an adult body. You grow taller, your voice changes, and your body develops new features. Everyone grows at their own pace - some people grow early and others later. Growth is controlled by hormones.

title: Newton's Laws of Motion
content: Newton's First Law: objects keep moving unless a force stops them. Second Law: Force = mass × acceleration. Third Law: every action has an equal reaction.

title: States of Matter
content: Matter has three main states. Solid has fixed shape. Liquid flows but has fixed volume. Gas expands to fill space. Water can be ice, liquid water, or steam.

title: Plant Life Cycle
content: Plants start as seeds. Seeds germinate in soil with water and sunlight. Seedlings grow roots and leaves. Mature plants produce flowers. Flowers become fruits with new seeds.

title: Animal Classification
content: Animals are grouped into classes. Mammals have fur and feed milk. Birds have feathers and lay eggs. Reptiles have scales and are cold-blooded. Fish live in water. Amphibians live on land and water.

title: The Human Skeleton
content: The human skeleton has 206 bones. The skull protects the brain. The ribcage protects the heart and lungs. The spine supports the body. Bones store minerals and make blood cells.

title: Elements and Compounds
content: Elements are pure substances like oxygen and iron. Compounds are elements bonded together like water (H2O) and salt (NaCl). The periodic table lists all 118 known elements.

title: Food Chains
content: Food chains show who eats what. Plants are producers. Herbivores eat plants. Carnivores eat other animals. Omnivores eat both. Decomposers break down dead matter.

title: Simple Circuits
content: A circuit needs a power source, wires, and a load. Current flows in a loop. Batteries provide DC power. Switches control the flow. Resistors limit current. LEDs light up.

title: The Rock Cycle
content: Rocks change over millions of years. Igneous rock forms from cooling magma. Sedimentary rock forms from compressed layers. Metamorphic rock changes with heat and pressure. The cycle continues forever.

title: Weather and Climate
content: Weather is what happens each day. Climate is the average weather over years. Temperature, wind, rain, and clouds make weather. The sun drives weather patterns. Climate change is long-term shifts.

title: The Five Senses
content: Humans have five senses. Eyes see light and color. Ears hear sound waves. Nose smells particles in air. Tongue tastes sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami. Skin feels touch, pressure, pain, and temperature.

title: Energy Types
content: Energy comes in many forms. Kinetic energy is movement. Potential energy is stored. Thermal energy is heat. Chemical energy is in food and fuel. Electrical energy powers devices. Energy cannot be created or destroyed.

title: The Digestive System
content: Digestion breaks down food. The mouth chews and adds saliva. The stomach churns and adds acid. The small intestine absorbs nutrients. The large intestine absorbs water. Waste leaves the body.

title: Day and Night
content: Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours. The side facing the sun has daytime. The side away from the sun has nighttime. Earths rotation causes sunrises and sunsets.

title: Light and Shadows
content: Light travels in straight lines. Objects block light creating shadows. Shadow size changes with light position. Morning and evening shadows are long. Noon shadows are short.
